extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, game developers, and general readers interested in video game copyright law
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used to evaluate whether one video game unlawfully copies another's protected expression (look-and-feel, art, hierarchy, dialogue) as applied in U.S. federal court decisions summarized by the Spry Fox v. Lolapps case. Useful for assessing substantial similarity, access, and which elements are protectable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea–expression distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects the expression of an idea, not the underlying idea itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must exclude the overall game 'idea' (for example, 'a game about matching objects' or general gameplay concepts) from protection, and focus on what is expressive about the work. The court excluded purely conceptual/common-game ideas while examining expressive implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial similarity (focus on similarities)
rubrics_metrics.description: A copyright issue 'must focus on what is similar, not what is different, when comparing two works.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing infringement, the court emphasizes shared expressive elements (e.g., object hierarchy, setting, theme, mechanics as expressed) rather than cosmetic differences. Similarities such as hierarchical progression of objects, presence of a wild creature affecting play, similar marketplaces and dialog language were treated as evidence of substantial similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scènes à faire (standard or stock elements excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain elements that naturally flow from or are standard to a genre are not protectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court excluded éléments such as using coins to track score and exchange for in-game advantages as scènes à faire. These are considered unprotectable because they are standard to the genre/idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional elements are not copyrightable
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely functional aspects of a game cannot be protected by copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples the court excluded include the six-by-six game grid. Functional mechanics or systems necessary for gameplay are treated differently from expressive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look-and-feel can be protected
rubrics_metrics.description: A game's 'look and feel' — its expressive combination of art, theme, layout, and mechanics presentation — may be protected by copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court affirmed that original games can be protected from clones based on overall look and feel, citing and applying reasoning from Tetris Holding, LLC v. Xio Interactive, Inc. Visual differences do not automatically defeat claims if the expressive look-and-feel is substantially similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access as a prerequisite to copying inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying is usually proved by showing the potential infringer had access to the original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of access (e.g., an existing non-disclosure agreement, prior working relationship, or admission of a 'similar match-3 style') supports an inference of copying. The existence of an NDA and prior development relationship was weighed heavily in Spry Fox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object hierarchy and setting/theme as expressive elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific hierarchy of objects and depiction of the field of play can constitute protectable expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progressions such as 'grass→bush→tree→hut' versus 'sapling→tree→tent→cabin' and the coupled depiction of the playfield (meadow vs snowfield) were treated as similar expressive choices that contribute to infringement analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game names similarity relevant but names not copyrighted
rubrics_metrics.description: A game's title is not technically copyrighted, but similarity in names can be relevant to substantial similarity/expertise in imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While names alone don't confer copyright protection, close similarity of titles may be considered as part of the totality of evidence when assessing copying or intent to imitate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may rely on screenshots and written descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A court can base its infringement analysis on screenshots and written descriptions rather than playing the games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Spry Fox the court did not play either game but accepted screenshots and descriptions as sufficient to identify expressive similarities. That means documentary visual evidence can be decisive at early stages (e.g., motion to dismiss).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party commentary and player perception as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Online commentators' observations or community reaction about similarity may be admissible evidence of substantial similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court accepted evidence from online commentators that the games were substantially similar, indicating that public perception can support an infringement claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishable art assets do not preclude infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where visual art assets differ (2D vs 3D, different characters/themes), infringement can still be found based on overall expressive similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spry Fox ruling noted that despite differences in presentation (e.g., pastoral vs snowy themes, bears vs yetis), the expressive commonalities could show appropriation — courts will look beyond surface art differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gameplay mechanics vs expressive implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure game mechanics/ideas are not copyrightable, but the particular expressive implementation of mechanics may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants' argument that basic gameplay is unprotectable (citing older cases like Data East v. Epyx) can be limited by modern precedent: courts may decline to treat expressive implementations of mechanics as mere ideas and can protect them where the expression is original and copied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior relationship / contract increases inference of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior working relationship (like being contracted to port a game) or having confidential access makes courts more likely to infer imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal scholars and practitioners cited the existence of an NDA and prior agreement to develop an iOS port as a major factor favoring Spry Fox; courts are more likely to find infringement when there is demonstrable evidence the defendant had both access and opportunity to imitate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to balance protection against over‑broad monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should aim to shut down egregious clones without granting monopolies over entire genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators cautioned (e.g., Stephen McArthur) that while protecting original work is important, judges must avoid decisions that would give one party exclusive rights over generic mechanics or entire categories of games; balance is required when delineating protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedential influence (Tetris v. Xio and evolution of judicial experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent rulings and judges' evolving familiarity with video games influence outcomes; Tetris v. Xio served as persuasive precedent protecting look-and-feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spry Fox applied reasoning from Tetris v. Xio and commentators observed courts are increasingly willing to apply look-and-feel analysis as judges gain more experience with video games, affecting how substantial similarity is evaluated.
